rows.title: Pupil
rows.text: If you are a lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar, snow leopard, cheetah, mountain lion or jaguarundi, the dark opening of each eye is a round circle, where a domestic cat's is a vertical slit. If you are a clouded leopard, your pupils are vertical. If you are a Sunda clouded leopard, you very likely have vertical pupils too, since the clouded leopard, your close relative, does.
rows.note: Clouded leopard (R9) has vertical pupils, unlike the other big cats, so the row names it separately.

rows.title: Clouded leopard
rows.text: When your pupils narrow in bright light, they close to a tall, thin slit. A published classification records vertical pupils in the clouded leopard, and the Sunda clouded leopard belongs to the same genus, Neofelis, so if you are a Sunda clouded leopard you very likely have them too.
rows.note: R1's quote is only a table row label ("Neofelis_nebulosa 322"), so the value "Vertical" rests on the record's value field. I left out slit width, pupil size and any claim about why the shape helps, since no record gives them.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: Cone cells that sense short wavelengths of light, called S cones, have been found in the eyes of a cheetah, a leopard and a bobcat. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have, or which colors they sense best. A dog, which is a carnivore like you, has two pigments that peak at about 430 and 555 nanometers.

cites.taxon: Acinonyx jubatus, Lynx rufus, Panthera pardus

rows.note: R1 shows S cones but gives no count of cone classes, so I did not state one for any cat.

rows.title: Cheetah
rows.text: If you are a cheetah, the color-sensing cells called M cones lie in a horizontal streak across your eye, the pattern also found in the pig and the deer, which live in open country. A compiled value puts your sharpness at about 25 cycles a degree, a little under the 30 a human reads on an eye chart.
rows.note: R1's method is not stated, so I gave the sharpness as a compiled value. R2 gives the streak but not that it is the sharpest region, so I did not say that.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a cheetah, a compilation of published values lists your eyesight at about 25 cycles a degree, a little below the 30 a human reads on an eye chart. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar or any other big cat. A textbook survey says only that the great cats have high visual acuity, and it gives no measurement.
rows.note: Cheetah value is a compiled figure with no method stated, rounded to about 25. The house cat figure (R1) was left out because acuity numbers do not travel across genera. The textbook year was dropped because it is not in the record.

rows.title: Dim light
rows.text: If you are a lion or a clouded leopard, your eyes have a tapetum lucidum, a layer in the eye that looks milky blue, and a lion's was the largest of the three cats examined in one study. Tigers, leopards, jaguars, snow leopards and Sunda clouded leopards very likely have one too, but nobody has looked for it in mountain lions, cheetahs or jaguarundis. Nobody has measured how little light you need to see.
rows.note: Left out the house cat figures (threshold up to 7 times lower than a human's, R2; tapetum reflects up to 130 times more light, R3) because numbers do not carry from house cats to big cats.

rows.title: Field of view and depth
rows.text: Nobody has measured how wide an area you take in at once, or how much of it both of your eyes see together. Both have been measured in the domestic cat, which belongs to a different genus, and those figures cannot be carried over to you.
rows.note: I left out all numbers. The two domestic cat records disagree on overlap (R1 implies about 60 degrees, R2 gives 140), and no record covers any big cat.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: The lens inside a house cat's eye lets ultraviolet light through, about 60 percent of the ultraviolet closest to violet in the six lenses measured. Nobody has measured the lens of a lion, tiger, leopard or any other big cat, so nobody knows how much ultraviolet light gets through yours.
rows.note: Lens optics travel only within a genus, so the house cat figure is not carried to big cats, despite the "rule 2" label in the species list. I left out any claim about UV-sensing cells, since no record covers them.
